JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. The present Appeal has been filed by M/s. BSL Limited (“Appellant”)
challenging the Impugned Order passed by Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory
Commission (“RERC”/ “Respondent No. 4”/ “State Commission”) order dated
23.04.2019 in Petition No. 1393/ 2018 (“Impugned Order”).
Description of the Parties
2. The Appellant, M/s. BSL Limited, is a company incorporated under the
Companies Act, 1956. It is a High Tension (HT) consumer of Respondent No.1,
Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (AVVNL) having a contracted demand of
6460 KVA.
3. Respondent No. 1, AVVNL is the distribution licensee responsible for supply of
electricity in its licensed area and is the entity which levied the disputed
wheeling charges.
4. Respondent No. 2, State Power Committee (SPC) is the Power Committee set
up under grid code specified by the State Commission.
Page 2 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
5. Respondent No. 3, Rajasthan Vidyut Prasaran Nigam Limited (RVPNL)/ State
Load Despatch Centre (SLDC) is the State transmission utility and the nodal
agency responsible for operation of the State grid and administration of open
access.
6. Respondent No. 4, Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission (RERC) is the
State Electricity Regulatory Commission constituted under the Electricity Act,
2003.
Factual Matrix of the Case
7. The State Commission had, from time to time, determined wheeling charges
under its tariff orders dated 19.09.2006, 31.03.2010 and 31.03.2011 and
subsequently notified the Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms
and Conditions for Determination of Tariff) Regulations, 2009 and 2014 as well
as the Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for
Open Access) Regulations, 2016.
8. The Appellant entered into a Wheeling and Banking Agreement dated
19.03.2013 with Inox Renewables Limited (developer) and AVVNL followed by
a Wheeling Agreement dated 20.03.2013 with Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Prasaran
Nigam Limited and Inox Renewables Limited for wheeling of electricity
generated from its captive wind power project.
9. In February and March 2018, the Appellant disputed the wheeling charges
levied by AVVNL and submitted representations alleging excess recovery.
10. AVVNL, by notice dated 22.03.2018 stated that the wheeling charges had
been levied in accordance with Regulation 15 of the RERC Open Access
Regulations, 2016. Aggrieved thereby, the Appellant invoked the dispute
resolution mechanism under the Open Access Regulations.
Page 3 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
11. The Appellant’s grievance was first rejected by the SLDC through
communication dated 01.06.2018. Thereafter, the Appellant preferred the
matter before the State Power Committee, which, by communication dated
18.09.2018, upheld the levy of wheeling charges by AVVNL.
12. Aggrieved by the decisions of the SLDC and the State Power Committee,
the Appellant filed Petition No. 1393 of 2018 before the RERC challenging the
recovery of wheeling charges under Regulation 15 of the RERC Open Access
Regulations, 2016.
13. By the Impugned Order dated 23.04.2019, RERC dismissed the petition and
upheld the methodology adopted by AVVNL for levy of wheeling charges.
Aggrieved thereby, the Appellant has preferred the present Appeal.
14. The Appellant has prayed for the following relief before us:
“i. Set aside the impugned order dated 23.04.2019 passed by the Ld.
Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission in OP No. 1393/2018;
ii. Direct the Respondent Discom to levy wheeling charges on actual injection
of energy as per the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2014;
iii. Any other relief as this Hon’ble Tribunal deems fit and proper.”
Submissions of the Appellant
15. The Appellant submitted that the RERC erred in applying the Rajasthan
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Open Access)
Regulations, 2016 (“OA Regulations, 2016”) to the Appellant despite the
Wheeling and Banking Agreement (WBA) dated 19.03.2013 expressly
providing that wheeling charges would be governed by the RERC Order dated
23.01.2009 as amended from time to time.
Page 4 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
16. The Impugned Order failed to recognize that the Tariff Regulations, 2014
were never repealed or superseded by the OA Regulations, 2016. Regulation
32 of the OA Regulations, 2016 repeals only the Rajasthan Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Open Access) Regulations,
2004 (“OA Regulations, 2004”) and not the Tariff Regulations, 2014.
Consequently, the unilateral application of the OA Regulations, 2016 to the
Appellant is unsustainable.
17. The Appellant submitted that the wheeling charges have been wrongly
computed on the basis of contracted capacity by presuming continuous 24-hour
consumption throughout the month whereas the Appellant consumes electricity
only for limited hours on certain days and not at all on several days. Such
computation is contrary to the WBA and the applicable RERC Regulations.
18. The impugned methodology increased the Appellant’s wheeling charges
from ₹ 2,82,245/- (calculated at 11 paise/kWh for FY 2016-17) to ₹ 19,27,200/-
imposing an additional liability of ₹ 16,44,954/-. Such levy is arbitrary, contrary
to the applicable regulations and violative of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
of India.
19. RERC erred in law by failing to harmoniously construe the Tariff Regulations,
2014 and the OA Regulations, 2016 thereby disregarding the settled principle
of harmonious construction and wrongly subjecting the Appellant to the OA
Regulations, 2016.
Submissions of the Respondent No. 1- AVVNL
20. AVVNL submitted that the Appellant is an Open Access consumer and upon
coming into force of the OA Regulations, 2016, wheeling charges became
payable on the basis of the Open Access capacity contracted or utilized,
whichever is higher and not on the basis of actual energy wheeled as was the
Page 5 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
practice under the OA Regulations, 2004. The RERC, by clarification dated
16.12.2016 also confirmed this interpretation.
21. The Wheeling and Banking Agreement binds the Appellant to future
regulatory amendments; Clause 11 (Change of Law) of the Wheeling and
Banking Agreement provides that any changes in applicable Acts, Policies,
Rules, Regulations or Regulatory Directions issued from time to time shall be
binding on all parties. Therefore, the Appellant is bound by the OA Regulations,
2016 which superseded the OA Regulations, 2004.
22. Regulation 15(1) of OA Regulations 2016 stipulates that transmission and
wheeling charges are payable on the basis of Open Access capacity contracted
or utilized, whichever is higher. Since Open Access is granted in terms of
capacity and not actual energy consumption, the wheeling charges on a
capacity basis are rightly levied. The Tariff Regulations merely prescribe the
applicable rate (Rs. /kWh) and do not alter the basis of computation prescribed
under the OA Regulations, 2016.
23. Regulation 32 of the OA Regulations, 2016 repealed the OA Regulations,
2004. Accordingly, when read together with Clause 11 of the WBA and
Regulation 15, the only applicable framework governing the Appellant is the OA
Regulations, 2016. Therefore, billing of wheeling charges under the OA
Regulations, 2016 is lawful and valid.
24. Annexure-3 (Part-IV General), Clause 29 of the Procedure for Grant of Open
Access under the OA Regulations, 2016 specifically provides that wheeling
charges shall be billed on the basis of Open Access capacity contracted or
utilized, whichever is higher thereby removing any ambiguity regarding the
method of computation.
Page 6 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
25. The State Commission had already decided the same issue in its order dated
13.12.2016 in the case of M/s. Shree Krishna Rolling Mills (Jaipur) Ltd. and the
impugned order dated 23.04.2019 applied the same principle to six consumers
including the Appellant.
26. Since the Appellant had agreed to be governed by the applicable Rules and
Regulations as amended from time to time and the wheeling charges were
levied strictly in accordance with the OA Regulations, 2016, the appeal is liable
to be dismissed.
Submissions of the Respondent Nos. 2 and 3
27. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 submitted that the Appellant is an Open Access
consumer and is governed by the OA Regulations, 2016. Regulation 15
expressly mandates that transmission and wheeling charges are payable on
the basis of the contracted open access capacity or the utilized open access
capacity, whichever is higher, and therefore the Appellant cannot seek levy of
wheeling charges on any other basis.
28. The Tariff Regulations are relevant only for determination of wheeling
charges for the State as a whole, whereas recovery of charges from individual
Open Access consumers is governed solely by OA Regulations, 2016.
Consequently, the Appellant’s reliance on the Tariff Regulations is misplaced.
29. Open Access is granted on the basis of sanctioned capacity and the
distribution system is reserved accordingly. Since capacity is allocated
irrespective of actual energy drawal, wheeling charges must necessarily be
levied on a capacity basis and not on actual energy wheeled or injected as
claimed by the Appellant.
30. Clause 29 of the Standard Agreement executed under the Open Access
Regulations expressly provides that wheeling charges shall be payable on the
Page 7 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
basis of the contracted open access capacity or the utilized capacity, whichever
is higher. The Appellant is bound by the terms of the agreement.
31. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 further submitted that RERC had settled the law
in this regard in the matters being Petition No. 604/16, 848/16 and 868/16 filed
by M/s. Shree Krishna Roiling Mills (Jaipur) Ltd., M/s. AMP Industries Ltd.,
Alwar, M/s. Shiva Steelage Pvt. Ltd., Jaipur respectively whereby RERC in its
order dated 13.12.2016 has categorically held that the wheeling charges have
to be levied under OA Regulations on contracted capacity or energy utilized by
an open access consumer, whichever is higher and not on any other basis.
32. While the Tariff Regulations prescribe the methodology for determination of
wheeling charges for the distribution system, the actual recovery from an Open
Access consumer must be in accordance with the Open Access Regulations.
The Commission rightly held that overall network utilization is relevant for tariff
determination whereas individual billing must follow the Open Access
Regulations.
Our Analysis and Conclusions
33. We note that the main grievance of the Appellant is application of wheeling
charges on the basis of capacity post implementation of OA Regulations, 2016,
which was earlier on the basis of energy. The contentions of the Appellant
essentially contain two limbs:
i. The wheeling agreement provided for application of the wheeling charges
in accordance with RERC orders issued from time to time and the same
cannot be altered later, and
ii. The OA Regulations, 2016 do not repeal of the RERC Tariff Regulations,
2014 and therefore, it is entitled for continued governance under the latter.
34. The relevant extract of the Wheeling and Banking Agreement (WBA) is
reproduced below:
Page 8 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
“5 (A) Transmission & Wheeling of Energy
Keeping in view the Grid Policy and amended from time to time the Power
Produce shall be free to use the power for their captive consumption at their unit
BSL LIMITED BHILWARA after paying the transmission & wheeling charges and
losses as per RERC order dated 23.01.2009 and amended from time to time.”
35. We note that the aforesaid clause of the WBA anchors the payment of
transmission and wheeling charges to the RERC order dated 23.01.2009.
Although the aforesaid clause refers to “RERC order dated 23.01.2009”, it is, in
fact, the RERC Regulations, namely, RERC (Terms and Conditions for
Determination of Tariff) Regulations, 2009 (“RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009”)
issued on 23.01.2009. Likewise, the expression “and amended from time to
time” is evidently intended to mean “as amended from time to time”. The clause,
therefore, unmistakably contemplates the application of the relevant
Regulations, as amended from time to time.
36. The RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009 are on the record. From Regulation 108
of these regulations (extracted in next paragraph of this judgment), we note that
provision in RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009 regarding wheeling charges for
open access customers was traceable to provision in OA Regulations, 2004.
Though OA Regulations, 2004 are not on record, they are available in public
domain (downloadable from webpage https://rerc.rajasthan.gov.in/rerc-user-
files/regulations., last accessed on 05.08.2026). We note that OA Regulations,
2004 were the first set of regulations on open access in intra-state transmission
and distribution system in Rajasthan and were issued by RERC in May 2004.
So far as wheeling charges are concerned, the relevant provision in the
aforesaid Regulations was as under:
“14. Charges for open access
(1) The Transmission charges or wheeling charges for use of the Transmission
System of the Transmission Licensee or the distribution system of a distribution
licensee shall be regulated as under:
Page 9 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
(a) Transmission charges and wheeling charges payable by an open access
customer shall be determined by the Commission in terms of the regulations
framed by the Commission for determination of tariff.
…..
…..”
37. It may be seen from the above extract that though OA Regulations, 2004
dealt with practically every aspect of open access, it left the issue of
determination of wheeling charges applicable to open access customers on
another set of Regulations namely terms and conditions of tariff. Accordingly,
the same was covered in the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009. The relevant part
of the Regulations relating to payment of transmission and wheeling charges
as contained in the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009 is extracted below:
“108. Applicability
…
(2) These Regulations shall also apply in determining tariff payable for
wheeling of electricity by a Distribution System User who has been allowed
open access to the distribution system of a Distribution Licensee in accordance
with the Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission (Open Access)
Regulations, 2004:”
“128. Wheeling charges
(1) …..
….
…..
(3) Payment of wheeling charges:
Wheeling charges may consist of the following or any one or combination
thereof:
(a) Fixed charge in Rs. per month per KW of contracted power.
(b) A charge in Rs. Per kWh of energy wheeled separately for
(i) Wire business
(ii) Installation, operation and maintenance of meters, metering system
and any other equipment at consumer’s premises.
(iii) Billing & collection of payment
Page 10 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
(iv) Consumer services.
(c) Connectivity fee.
(d) Reactive energy charge / incentive
……”
38. It is evident from the above extract that the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009
also governed open access customers in respect of wheeling charges. These
Regulations provided that wheeling charges could be levied as a fixed charge
based on capacity, or as an energy-based charge, or as a combination of the
two. Thereafter, based on the aforesaid Regulations, RERC issued orders
dated 31.03.2010 and later order dated 31.03.2011, inter-alia covering
determination of wheeling charges. Both these orders determined wheeling
charges on Rs. per kWh basis. This clearly indicates that the wheeling charges
were actually determined by RERC based on energy wheeled and not capacity.
39. The Subsequent regulations, namely RERC Tariff Regulations, 2014
replaced RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009. The provisions of the RERC Tariff
Regulations 2014 governing wheeling charges were materially identical with the
corresponding provisions contained in the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009.
40. Subsequently, RERC framed new regulations relating to open access,
namely OA Regulations, 2016 with express repeal of OA Regulations, 2004
(regulation 32 of the OA Regulations, 2016). Unlike OA Regulations, 2004, the
OA Regulations, 2016 covered the issue of wheeling charges also. The relevant
extract of these Regulations is reproduced below:
“15. Charges for Open Access
(1) The open access customer shall pay the transmission charges and wheeling
charges as determined from time to time.
Provided that the transmission and wheeling charges shall be payable on the
basis of open access capacity contracted or open access capacity utilized
whichever is higher. The excess open access capacity utilized up to 5% of open
access capacity allocation occurring to the extent of two time blocks of 15 minutes
each during a month shall be exempted.”
Page 11 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
41. It may be seen from the above extract that there is clear shift in the approach
relating to basis of wheeling charges; the OA Regulations, 2016 stipulated
wheeling charges on the basis of capacity contracted or actual capacity utilized,
whichever is higher.
42. In this background, we proceed to examine the first limb of the Appellant’s
argument that the subsequent Regulations could not alter the basis for the levy
of wheeling charges as stipulated in the WBA. We find no merit in this
contention. It is well settled that statutory regulations, being subordinate
legislation, prevail over contractual stipulations to the extent of any
inconsistency and, therefore, make inroads into the terms of a contract (PTC
India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, (2010) 4 SCC 603). The
OA Regulations, 2016 expressly stipulated that wheeling charges were to be
determined on the basis of capacity and would, therefore, ordinarily prevail over
any contrary provision contained in the WBA. Moreover, as we have analysed
in the earlier part of this Judgement, the WBA itself contemplates the application
of the Regulations, as amended from time to time.
43. Now coming to the second limb of the argument of the Appellant, it is
understandable that the Appellant desires to continue to be governed under
RERC Tariff Regulations, 2014 as the wheeling charges payable by it would
increase under OA Regulations, 2016 mainly due to shift from energy-based
application to capacity-based application. However, this desire has to be
supported by legally tenable argument. We now proceed to examine merits in
this contention of the Appellant that the OA Regulations do not explicitly repeal
RERC Tariff Regulations, 2014 and hence they continue to apply to them
specially since they were mentioned in WBA.
44. A crucial aspect that needs attention is that both the RERC Tariff
Regulations, 2009 and the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2014 were framed to lay
Page 12 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
down the terms and conditions for determination of tariff based on cost-of-
service model but derived the authority to prescribe the methodology for
determination of wheeling charges for open access customers from the OA
Regulations 2004 (Regulation 14 (1) (a) extracted in paragraph 36 of this
judgment). Therefore, it is not surprising that only one or two sub-regulations
dealing with determination of wheeling charges for open access were related to
open access in the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009 and the RERC Tariff
Regulations, 2014. These regulations did not deal with procedural aspects
about who is eligible for open access, various categories of open access, the
method of applying for open access etc. On the other hand, the OA Regulations,
2016 is a complete code on intra-State open access because it
comprehensively governs the entire field viz. eligibility, charges, procedures,
priority, curtailment, metering, scheduling, settlement, dispute resolution and
specifically determination of wheeling charges, which was not part of OA
Regulations, 2004.
45. The Appellant itself has admitted that OA Regulations, 2016 explicitly
repealed OA Regulations, 2004. This is amply clear from the Regulation 32:
“32. Repeal and Savings
(1) On commencement of these Regulations, the Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions for Open Access) Regulations, 2004 shall stand
repealed.
Provided that the application for grant of open access under these Regulations may
be made as per the procedure issued under the old Regulations till new procedure
is issued under the provisions of these Regulations.
(2) On commencement of these Regulations, any reference to the Rajasthan
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Open Access)
Regulations, 2004 in any of the Regulations, standards, codes or procedures of the
Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission shall be deemed to be replaced by
Rajasthan Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Open
Access) Regulations, 2016.
….
…….”
Page 13 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
46. In view of the above, we are unable to accept the contention that the mere
continuation of the RERC Tariff Regulations, 2014 would preserve their
application for determining the basis of wheeling charges payable by an open
access consumer. The RERC Tariff Regulations, 2009 and 2014 derived their
relevance to open access wheeling charges from the framework contained in
the OA Regulations, 2004 which specifically contemplated that the transmission
and wheeling charges payable by an open access customer would be
determined in terms of the regulations framed by the Commission for terms and
conditions of tariff.
47. However, with the commencement of the OA Regulations, 2016, the OA
Regulations, 2004 stood expressly repealed under Regulation 32, and
Regulation 32(2) further provided that every reference to the OA Regulations,
2004 in the regulations, standards, codes or procedures of the Commission
would be deemed to be replaced by a reference to the OA Regulations, 2016.
Consequently, the legal basis under which the 2009 and 2014 Tariff Regulations
operated in the field of open access wheeling charges could no longer be
invoked to determine the governing regime for open access after the OA
Regulations, 2016 came into force.
48. The OA Regulations, 2016, being the subsequent and comprehensive
regulatory framework governing intra-State open access, expressly and
specifically provides under Regulation 15 the basis on which transmission and
wheeling charges are payable, namely, the open access capacity contracted or
the open access capacity utilized, whichever is higher. Thus, while the Tariff
Regulations, 2009 and 2014 may not have been expressly repealed by the OA
Regulations, 2016, they cannot, after the repeal of the OA Regulations, 2004,
be relied upon as the source of authority for determining the basis of wheeling
charges payable under the open access regime which is specifically governed
by the OA Regulations, 2016.
Page 14 of 15

Judgement in Appeal No.142 of 2021
49. In view of the foregoing analysis, we have come to the conclusion that there
is no merit in the arguments put forward by the Appellant assailing the
Impugned Order.
ORDER
For the foregoing reasons as stated above, we have come to the conclusion that
the Appeal No. 142 of 2021 is devoid of merit and is accordingly dismissed. As a
corollary, the Impugned Order dated 23.04.2019 passed by the Rajasthan
Electricity Regulatory Commission in Petition No. 1393/2018 is hereby affirmed.
PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT ON THIS 11th DAY OF AUGUST, 2026.
(Ajay Talegaonkar) (Virender Bhat)
Technical Member Judicial Member

JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. The present Appeal has been filed by the Appellant Damodar Valley Power
Consumers’ Association (“DVPCA”) and its members challenging the Impugned
Order dated 24.03.2025 passed by the West Bengal Electricity Regulatory
Commission (“WBERC”/ “Respondent No. 1”/ “State Commission”) in Case No.
APR(R)-33/23-24.
2. In this appeal, one of the issues being raised by the Appellant- DVPCA is
related to interest on differential Annual Fixed Charges (AFC) for the period 2019-
Page 6 of 10

Judgement in Appeal No. 18 of 2026
20. The essential facts of the case on the issue of interest on differential AFC are
similar to that in Appeal No. 15 of 2026, except that the controversy is for a
differeny year. The principal question that arose for consideration in Appeal No.
15 of 2026, as also in the present appeal, is whether the methodology adopted by
the WBERC for determing the interest on differential AFC was correct.
3. In the Appeal No. 15 of 2026 also, other issues were raised in the appeal.
However, learned counsels for the parties had agreed that since submissions
which were made on the issue of interest on differential AFC during the course of
hearing on the interim application were similar which would be made at the time of
final disposal of the appeal on that issue; and had requested that the appeal may
be disposed of with the liberty to approach this Tribunal with remaining issues, if
so desired by the Appellant. Accordingly, we had procedded to deal with that
appeal and the judgement was delivered on 02.07.2026. In the said judgement
after a detailed analysis, this Tribunal had upheld the order of WBERC which was
impugned in that appeal.
4. During the hearing held on 21.07.2026 in the present case, Mr. Shri
Venkatesh, learned counsel for the DVC submitted that one of the issues raised in
the appeal relating to interest on differential AFC was also involved in Appeal No.
15 of 2026 which has been disposed of by this Tribunal vide judgment dated
02.07.2026 and therefore, this appeal may also be decided in terms of the said
previous judgment giving liberty to the Appellant to raise the remaining issues by
way of a fresh appeal.
5. Responding to this, Mr. Rajiv Yadav, learned counsel for the Appellant
submitted that even though the Appellant may not be in agreement with the final
conclusion of this Tribunal in the said Appeal No. 15 of 2026, yet, in view of the
Page 7 of 10

Judgement in Appeal No. 18 of 2026
observations of this Tribunal in paragraph 37 of the said judgment, this Tribunal
may consider if the instant appeal can be decided in the light of the observations
and conclusions arrived at in the said judgment. To a pointed query as to whether
the findings in the judgment dated 02.07.2026 in Appeal No. 15 of 2026 on the
issue of interest on differential AFC is applicable to this appeal, the learned counsel
avoided a direct or specific answer. He submitted that he leaves it to the wisdom
of this Tribunal to decide as to whether the judgment in Appeal No. 15 of 2026 is
applicable to the instant appeal and the instant appeal may be decided
accordingly.
6. While we have no quarrel with the submission of the Appellant that it is not
in agreement with the final conclusion reached in the judgment in Appeal No. 15
of 2026, we consider it appropriate to briefly note the circumstances in which the
concluding part of paragraph 37 of the judgment dated 02.07.2026 came to be
incorporated, having regard to the submissions advanced by the learned counsel
for the Appellant. We find it appropriate to first extract the said paragraph here:
“37. We have already concluded under Issue 1 that the AFC order
had not attained finality. In regard to contention of DVC that the
Appellants have covered these issues in the appeals selectively only
for the years when revised AFC had reduced from original AFC,
during the hearing, Ld. Counsel for the Appellants Mr. Rajiv Yadav
had clarified that in-principle they do not agree with the methodology
of truing up based on empirical formula for all the years, but had no
ground to object to it in the years in which they had gained financially
due to such adjustment clear that the application of the “Empirical
formula” has benefitted consumers in some years and to the DVC in
other years, and therefore, the apprehension of DVPCA is
Page 8 of 10

Judgement in Appeal No. 18 of 2026
unfounded that this formula was devised after realizing that the
trued-up AFC was lower than the AFC considered in the original tariff
order. Whatever conclusion we arrive at in this Appeal, may get
applied consistently in all those years where the relevant orders
have been challenged before us in the form of Appeals.”
7. It may be seen that the concluding sentence of paragraph 37 was made in
the context of the submissions recorded in the earlier part of the said paragraph.
There were multiple appeals inter-alia concerning the issue of interest on
differential AFC, albeit pertaining to different periods. During certain years,
however, the Appellants were not adversely affected, as the truing-up exercise
resulted in a reduction in the interest on differential AFC. Ordinarily, there would
have been no necessity to specifically include the concluding sentence in the
judgment, since, for the years in which the interest on differential AFC had
increased, the issue would have arisen in the relevant appeals and, consistent with
the precedent, the same conclusion would naturally have followed. However, the
peculiar factual and procedural situation, as is evident from the rival submissions
of the Appellants and the Respondents, necessitated the inclusion of the
concluding sentence. This was because, for the years in which the interest on
differential AFC had reduced, the issue did not arise in the appeals concerned, the
Appellants having no grievance in those years. In the absence of such an express
clarification, the benefit of parity flowing from the earlier decision would not have
automatically extended to those years.
8. Based on the foregoing discussion, in the present case also, we uphold
the methodology adoted by the WBERC in the Impugned Order determining
interest on differential AFC. In so far as other issues are concerned, the Appellants
are given liberty to agitate those issues by way of fresh appeal.
